metadata.title: Education systems, education reforms, and adult skills in the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PIAAC microdata (2012 and 2014 rounds) and explicitly states that analyses account for both sampling error and the variance introduced by plausible-value imputation of proficiency scores. The paper does not report the specific PIAAC weight variable names (e.g., student design weights) or whether replicate-weight methods were used, so the exact weighting implementation cannot be verified from the text provided. The analytic samples are restricted to adults aged 20–35 (for correlational models) and to 17 European countries for the reform analysis, with additional exclusions based on missing reform indicators (e.g., tracking index availability) and missing education-system indices. Because the paper does not describe any ML-specific unweighting choice, weighting should be assumed to follow standard PIAAC analysis practice in the OECD public data products, but the manuscript text here does not document the exact weight variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that proficiency scores are represented by 10 plausible values and that analyses account for both sampling error and the variance due to plausible-value imputation, but it does not describe how missing questionnaire or background variables were handled beyond including missing-data dummy variables for parental education and immigration status. This means the missing-data strategy is only partially documented (reporting gap for the exact treatment of missingness in regression estimation). Given that the study relies on regression models with fixed effects and missingness indicators, the precise missing-data handling method (e.g., listwise deletion vs. imputation) cannot be determined from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Two analytic subsamples are used. For the correlational analysis of education-system characteristics (tracking and vocational education orientation), the sample is restricted to adults aged 20–35 in 27 PIAAC-participating countries matched to education-system measures around 2002; respondents who had lived in the surveyed country for less than five years are excluded, yielding 53,831 observations across 27 countries (with Estonia excluded from the tracking-index model and New Zealand excluded from the vocational-orientation model due to missing education-system indices). For the reform analysis, the sample is restricted to adults aged 20–35 across 17 European countries where education reform data are available (tracking-age changes and university-access expansion reforms), using all birth cohorts in PIAAC for this step, yielding 102,391 observations across the 17 European countries.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes adult numeracy skills using PIAAC microdata from the 2012 and 2014 rounds, where proficiency in literacy and numeracy is represented by 10 plausible values derived from calibrated and scaled cognitive item responses. The study first conducts correlational analyses linking country-level education-system characteristics (early tracking and vocational education orientation, constructed from cross-national education data around 2002) to average numeracy/literacy levels and percentile gaps for adults aged 20–35. It then estimates long-run associations of two reform types in 17 European countries—postponing tracking age and expanding university access for vocational-track students—using OLS and unconditional quantile regression to examine effects across the numeracy distribution (10th to 90th percentiles). The report finds that vocationally oriented systems are associated with higher average numeracy and more compressed upper-tail dispersion, while tracking-age postponement shows no significant average effect but benefits lower percentiles. Expanding university access is associated with higher numeracy, especially for individuals in the bottom deciles, reducing skill gaps. The manuscript does not document the exact missing-data handling beyond including missingness dummies for some background variables, and it does not present ML model performance metrics because the analysis is econometric rather than predictive ML.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD report using econometric regression and quantile regression (OLS and unconditional quantile regression) rather than machine-learning predictive modeling. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract and no ML-style main findings table is populated. The report is still empirical and uses PIAAC plausible values, but the provided text does not support extracting ML-specific performance metrics or a target-variable ML pipeline.
